title: Fix “teh” to read “the”.
hint: Delete the e with x, then put it after the h with p.
why: Deleting a character stores it in a register. xp puts it after the next character, swapping adjacent letters.

title: Rename “count” to “total”, keeping the comma.
hint: At the start of count, cw changes the word without consuming the comma.
why: For a word under the cursor, cw changes through its end. Punctuation makes a useful boundary for a small rename.

title: Remove the “--verbose” flag.
hint: daW removes the whitespace-delimited WORD and its following space.
why: The around-WORD object includes the hyphens and the separating space. The remaining command keeps exactly one space.

title: Change the first CSV field to “Mina”.
hint: ct, changes up to the next comma, keeping the comma.
why: A delimiter is a better boundary than a word when a field may contain spaces. This change preserves the rest of the row.

title: Swap the first two lines.
hint: dd cuts the line. After it disappears, p puts it below the current line.
why: Delete and put compose into a move. You don’t need a separate cut command.

title: Overwrite the three-letter month without disturbing the date.
hint: Use R, type Oct, then Escape.
why: Replace mode overwrites consecutive characters; this fixed-width field is a good fit.

title: Change the first comma to a colon.
hint: f followed by a character finds its next occurrence on the same line.
why: f, lands directly on the comma. rb would replace it with b; here r: makes it a colon.

title: Delete only the indentation before the heading.
hint: Use 0d^.
why: Deleting from column zero to the first nonblank character removes indentation alone.

title: Comment out the indented “return” line.
hint: I inserts before the first nonblank character, preserving the two-space indentation.
why: I targets the start of the content, not column zero. That distinction keeps an indented comment aligned with its block.

title: Empty the parentheses.
hint: di( deletes inside the surrounding parentheses.
why: The inner object keeps its delimiters. The same pattern works with brackets and braces.

title: Add a semicolon to each of the three statements.
hint: A; followed by Escape makes the first edit. Move down and use dot on each remaining line.
why: A records an end-of-line insertion, so dot works even when the lines have different lengths.

title: Change the colon after “port” to “=”.
hint: Capital F searches backward on the current line. F: finds the nearest colon to the left.
why: Backward character search is useful when the cursor has already passed the edit. Lowercase f would look in the wrong direction.

title: Indent both statements inside the block by two spaces.
hint: V selects the current line, j includes the next, and > indents both.
why: Visual line selection makes the scope visible before a block operation. The closing brace is deliberately excluded.

title: Replace the file path with “src/app.ts”.
hint: Capital W treats the entire non-space path as one WORD. Use ciW.
why: iw stops at punctuation; iW includes slashes and dots. Choose the object that matches the whole value you want to replace.

title: Delete the two leading path components.
hint: Use d2f/.
why: A counted find includes the second slash in the deletion.

title: Raise the shard count from 9 to 12, leaving replicas alone.
hint: Use 3 Ctrl+A from the beginning of the line.
why: Ctrl+A finds the next number on the current line.

title: Delete everything before the semicolon.
hint: dt; deletes up to, but not including, the semicolon.
why: t stops just before a character. Pair it with d to express a precise boundary without counting.

title: Change the suffix “Name” to “Id”.
hint: The cursor is on N. ce changes from here to the end of the word.
why: ce can replace just a suffix. ciw would replace the entire identifier, including the user prefix.

title: Put “// ” at absolute column zero, preserving the call’s original indentation.
hint: Use gI rather than I to insert before indentation.
why: gI targets column zero; I targets the first nonblank character.

title: Change only the second comma to a semicolon.
hint: 2f, finds the second comma. r; replaces that one character.
why: A count can select the second occurrence of a delimiter. Other separators stay unchanged.

title: Delete the final path segment, keeping its slash.
hint: Use F/ to find the preceding slash, l to move past it, then D.
why: The slash stays intact while D removes the entire remaining segment.

title: Join the path without adding a space.
hint: gJ joins with the next line without inserting a space.
why: J is right for prose; gJ is right when adjacent pieces must touch, such as a split path or identifier.

title: Replace only the nested parentheses contents with “user”.
hint: Use ci( within load(...), type user, then Escape.
why: The inner object chooses the nearest enclosing pair.

title: Indent the two nonadjacent return statements once.
hint: Indent this line with >>, move down two lines, then dot.
why: Separate navigation from the repeated change to skip untouched lines.

title: Convert the two-line robot greeting into one line with a colon.
hint: Append a colon before joining the next line.
why: J supplies the one separating space.

title: Delete the parenthetical aside and the extra separating space.
hint: Delete around the parenthetical aside, then remove one remaining space.
why: Use sentence, paragraph, and line boundaries to edit prose without counting every character.

title: Change the text inside the quotes.
hint: ci" changes everything inside the quotes while keeping the quotes.
why: Text objects describe what to edit. ci" saves you from counting characters or locating both ends.

title: Replace only the inner list with “ready”.
hint: Use ci[ while inside the list.
why: The nearest bracket object is independent of the surrounding function arguments.

title: Remove the two redundant “really” modifiers.
hint: Delete a word with dw, move to the next line with j0, then press dot.
why: The dot command repeats the last change at a new location.

title: Empty the button without removing its disabled attribute.
hint: Use dit inside the button text.
why: Deleting inside a tag preserves its attributes and delimiters.

title: Remove the first sentence and its separating spaces.
hint: Use das from inside the first sentence.
why: Around-sentence deletion includes its trailing separator, leaving the next sentence at the start.

title: Uppercase the complete dotted constant.
hint: Use gUiW.
why: The inner-WORD object includes dots because they are not whitespace.

title: Change both quoted milk choices to “oat”, skipping the roast setting.
hint: Change inside the first quotes, move down two lines, and repeat.
why: Dot repeats the text-object edit, not the navigation.

title: Clear the inner object without changing the outer one.
hint: Use di{ inside the nested object.
why: Cursor placement chooses the nearest enclosing brace pair.

title: Replace the complete single-quoted token with the unquoted word null.
hint: Use ca'null and Escape.
why: Changing around the quotes allows a different representation of the value.

title: Change the single-quoted value to “production”.
hint: ci' changes only the text inside single quotes.
why: The text object follows the delimiter you name. The assignment and quotes remain unchanged.

title: Uppercase the emphasis text while keeping its markup.
hint: Use gUit inside small.
why: A case operator can act on an inner-tag object.

title: Increase both limits by two using dot repeat.
hint: Increment the first number by two, move down, then repeat the change.
why: Locate the intended numeric field first, then use counted arithmetic to preserve its surrounding syntax.

title: Delete the final note paragraph but keep the blank separator before it.
before:
Main text.

Old note.
More old notes.
hint: Use dip inside the note paragraph.
why: An inner paragraph excludes surrounding blank separators.

title: Append “.value” immediately after the nested call.
hint: Use % from the outer opener, then a.value.
why: Matching-pair navigation reaches the correct closer despite nested parentheses.

title: Replace both two-word placeholders with “OK”.
hint: Change two words with c2w, type OK, Escape; repeat on the next line.
why: Dot remembers the complete change, including the inserted text.

title: Replace the middle paragraph with a one-line summary.
before:
Intro.

Long explanation.
More details.

End.
hint: Use cip inside the middle paragraph, type Summary., then Escape.
why: An inner paragraph spans its nonblank lines while preserving the surrounding blank lines.

title: Open the two locked doors while keeping the stone walls.
hint: Select the two lock characters and replace them with spaces.
why: Spaces are real replacement characters even when the result looks empty.

title: Uppercase only the middle paragraph.
before:
Introduction.

Handle with care.
Keep it dry.

Conclusion.
after:
Introduction.

HANDLE WITH CARE.
KEEP IT DRY.

Conclusion.

why: The inner-paragraph object selects its text without including the surrounding blank lines.

title: Remove the “temp.” prefix from three property accesses.
hint: Delete through the dot, then move to the next access and repeat twice.
why: Record an edit once, then navigate independently to repeat exactly that change.

title: Replace the inner array with a call to “getSnacks()”, removing its brackets.
hint: Change around the array rather than just inside it.
why: The new expression has its own delimiters, so the old brackets must go.

title: Remove the whispered aside and end the library instruction with an exclamation mark.
hint: Remove the aside and extra space, then replace the final period.
why: The aside and punctuation changes revise the tone while preserving the actual instruction.

title: Add “await ” before both indented calls.
hint: I inserts at the first nonblank character; repeat with j dot.
why: I preserves existing indentation when adding a prefix.

title: Invert the case of the mixed-case flag only.
hint: Use g~iw inside the flag.
why: g~ toggles each letter’s case instead of forcing the whole object to uppercase or lowercase.

title: Change the Markdown link destination while preserving its label.
hint: Find the parenthesis and change only its inner text.
why: Combine small, focused operators while leaving the surrounding code untouched.

title: Uppercase the next whole-word “warn”, leaving “warning” unchanged.

warn start
warning text
warn disk
after:
warn start
warning text
WARN disk

why: Whole-word search skips longer words with the same prefix.

TODO tests
checkpoint
TODO cleanup
after:

checkpoint
TODO cleanup

title: Replace the middle “:” with “=” after overshooting to the last one.
hint: Use f: and two semicolons to reach the last colon; comma reverses the find once, then r=.
why: Comma reverses the most recent character-find direction, which is useful for correcting an overshoot.

title: Remove the exact closing marker, preserving the longer marker name.
hint: Search for ^END$, then dd.
why: Both anchors distinguish an exact marker from a longer identifier.

title: Rename the next standalone “data”, then the following one, leaving “database”.
hint: Use * to find the next whole word, change it, then n dot.
why: Search direction and repeat commands let you choose an occurrence without editing every match.

title: Remove the three trailing semicolons from this line.
hint: Delete the first semicolon, repeat the find and deletion twice.
why: Record an edit once, then navigate independently to repeat exactly that change.

title: Change the middle “draft” label to “final”.
before:
draft intro
draft body
draft appendix
after:
draft intro
final body
draft appendix
hint: Use * then n to reach the last match; N steps back to the middle.
why: N reverses the direction of the current search for a single movement.

title: Remove the line containing the literal “[skip]” marker.
hint: Escape the square brackets in /\[skip\], then dd.
why: Regex metacharacters need escaping when you want their literal text.

title: Remove “https:” from the URL.
hint: df: deletes through the colon, including it.
why: f includes the found character when used with d. Compare that with dt:, which would leave the colon behind.

title: Remove the literal “.tmp” suffix from the matching filename only.
hint: Search for a literal dot followed by tmp at line end, then D.
why: Escaping the dot prevents it from acting as a wildcard.

title: Uppercase the first sentence, keeping the second unchanged.
hint: Use gUis inside the first sentence.
why: The inner-sentence object scopes the case operator to a grammatical unit.

title: Remove the last diagnostic line before the footer.
before:
DEBUG early
INFO ready
DEBUG final
FOOTER
hint: From the footer, search backward for ^DEBUG and delete that line.
why: Searching backward from a known endpoint selects the final matching record.

title: Uppercase the earlier “warn” label, leaving the current one alone.
before:
warn early
info middle
warn late
after:
WARN early
info middle
warn late
hint: Use # to find the preceding whole-word match, then gUiw.
why: Search direction controls which occurrence receives the operator.

title: Keep the colon but replace the key with “timeout”.
hint: Use ct:timeout, then Escape.
why: t stops before the delimiter so the replacement does not consume it.

title: Replace the quoted value on the “region” line with “east”.
hint: Search for ^region, then ci" changes its quoted value.
why: Search by a stable key rather than by a value that appears elsewhere.

title: Delete the line immediately above the END marker.
before:
keep
remove this note
END
footer
hint: Search for the exact marker, move up, and delete that line.
why: A nearby stable marker can identify the edit location when the text to remove has no useful pattern.

title: Change the outer square brackets to parentheses, preserving the nested list.
hint: Use %r) to change the matching closer, then 0r( to change the opener.
why: Matching pairs identifies the outer closer without disturbing the nested brackets.

title: Remove the actual “console.log” call, keeping “consoleXlog”.
hint: Search for console\.log, then dd.
why: Escaping the dot prevents it from matching any arbitrary character between console and log.

title: After finding the next marker, go back and delete the original marker line.
hint: Search forward, reverse once with N, then delete.
why: Search direction and repeat commands let you choose an occurrence without editing every match.

title: Change the value on the line containing literal “a.b”, preserving “axb”.
hint: Escape the dot in the search before changing the value.
why: Use a distinctive pattern to locate the record, then a local motion or object to perform the edit.

title: Replace only the final “pending” status on its line.
before:
pending review
status: pending
pending queue
after:
pending review
status: ready
pending queue

why: $ anchors the match to the end of a line.

hint: Search backward for ^chapter, then gUU uppercases its line.
why: An anchored backward search is useful when editing a section from somewhere inside it.

title: Change the hyphenated package name without changing its version.
hint: Use ct@new-package.
why: A delimiter motion treats a punctuation-rich identifier as one field.

title: Clear the arguments only on the call marked “retry”.
hint: Find retry, return to line start, then clear inside the call.
why: Use a distinctive pattern to locate the record, then a local motion or object to perform the edit.

title: Change the timeout only in the staging block.
hint: Find the staging heading, move to its setting, and change the value.
why: Use a distinctive pattern to locate the record, then a local motion or object to perform the edit.

title: Copy “customer_id” into the empty argument list.
hint: yiw copies the identifier. On the next line, f( finds the opening parenthesis; p puts after it.
why: A characterwise yank fits inside an existing line. This combines an object for copying with a character search for placement.

title: Open the recipe buffer without changing either file.
after: Workspace goal: Open the recipe buffer without changing either file.
hint: Use :bnext to visit the next loaded buffer.
why: A buffer holds file contents; one window can display different buffers.

title: Replace the word “wrong” with the earlier yanked “correct”.
hint: Yank the first word, select the second with viw, and put over it.
why: Putting over a visual selection replaces the selected text.

title: Open guide.txt beside main.js, with the guide active on the left.
after: Workspace goal: Open guide.txt beside main.js, with the guide active on the left.
hint: Use :vsplit guide.txt.
why: With default Vim split placement, a vertical split opens to the left.

title: Delete “obsolete” and copy “template” below “final”.
hint: yy copies template. j"_dd deletes obsolete into the black-hole register; p still puts template.
why: The black-hole register discards a deletion without replacing your copied text. The result accepts any route; this route practices preserving a yank.

title: Remove the nested emphasis but keep the surrounding link.
hint: Use dat from inside this.
why: Around-tag deletion removes the whole em element. The leading space inside the element is removed along with the emphasized text.

title: Open config.json by name, leaving the notes alone.
after: Workspace goal: Open config.json by name, leaving the notes alone.
hint: Use :buffer config.json.
why: Naming a loaded buffer is more reliable than counting through a long list.

title: Copy the quoted string, including quotes, into the empty assignment.
hint: Use ya" inside the string, then j$p.
why: Around-quotes copies the syntax as well as the value.

title: Focus main.js in the right pane without closing the guide.
after: Workspace goal: Focus main.js in the right pane without closing the guide.
hint: Press Ctrl+w, then l.
why: Window navigation combines Ctrl+w with familiar direction keys.

title: Delete the draft row, then paste the original yank below the body.
hint: Yank TITLE, delete draft, then use "0p.
why: Register 0 retains the most recent yank even after a deletion replaces the unnamed register.

title: Change the second colon to “=”.
hint: f: finds the first colon; semicolon repeats that find. Then r= replaces it.
why: The semicolon repeats the last character search. It is useful when you discover the right occurrence by moving through delimiters.

title: Copy the header below the body while deleting the obsolete row.
hint: Save the header in register a, delete obsolete, then put from a.
why: A named register keeps important text safe when another deletion changes the unnamed register.

title: Move the parenthesized group after the equals sign on the next line.
hint: Delete around parentheses, then put after the equals sign.
why: A deletion can serve as a cut operation for a delimited group.

title: Change both “cold” words to “warm”.
hint: Change the first word with ciw. Move to the other cold with WW, then press dot.
why: The dot command repeats your last change, including the inserted text. Make one useful change, then reuse it.

title: Visit the menu, then return to the alternate buffer: orders.txt.
after: Workspace goal: Visit the menu, then return to the alternate buffer: orders.txt.
hint: Use :buffer menu.txt, then :buffer # to return.
why: The alternate buffer is the file you most recently left.

title: Copy “BOO!” into the empty sign without stealing its exclamation mark.
hint: Yank to line end rather than yanking just a word.
why: A characterwise line-end yank includes punctuation.

title: Collect the two separated command lines and paste them below RUN.
after:
build
# note
test
RUN
build
test
hint: Yank build into a; append test with uppercase A; put register a below RUN.
why: Uppercase register names append to an existing named register instead of replacing it.

title: Indent only the final three statements once.
hint: Move to the first statement, then >G.
why: A shift operator can use an end-of-file motion.

title: Copy the inner parentheses into the empty square brackets.
hint: Yank inside parentheses, move to [, and put after it.
why: Text objects copy content without bringing the original delimiters.

title: Uppercase the entire quoted warning, including both words.
hint: Select inside the quotes and uppercase.
why: The selection follows the string boundaries rather than a word count.

title: Return to the marked column and replace the first digit with 9.
hint: Set mark a with ma, move away, return with backtick-a, then r9.
why: Backtick returns to the exact marked column, not just the line.

title: Keep the first word in register a while replacing the final word with it.
hint: Yank source into a, select the last word, and put a over it.
why: Use visual selections for replacement shapes and registers for preserving text across edits.

title: Remove scratch.txt from the buffer list; keep both project files loaded.
after: Workspace goal: Remove scratch.txt from the buffer list; keep both project files loaded.
hint: Use :bdelete on the scratch buffer.
why: Deleting a buffer removes it from the list; it does not delete the file from disk.

title: Remove the emphasis wrapper but keep “urgent”.
hint: Yank the inner text, select around the tag, and put over it.
why: Tag objects find matching elements and preserve surrounding markup, including nested tags.

title: Copy “Moon Spoon” into the empty sign and save it, keeping both panes.
after: Workspace goal: Copy “Moon Spoon” into the empty sign and save it, keeping both panes.
hint: Yank the title with 0y$, move right with Ctrl+w l, then f"p and :write.
why: Registers let you move text between windows without retyping it.

title: Remove the two-character gutter from all three lines.
hint: Ctrl+v starts a block; 2j extends down and l includes the second column. d removes the rectangle.
why: A block selection edits columns across rows without selecting whole lines.

title: Remove the current line and the following two lines.

keep
old a
old b
old c

why: The current line and a relative endpoint form an inclusive three-line range.

title: Open notes.txt above the recipe, keeping both visible.
after: Workspace goal: Open notes.txt above the recipe, keeping both visible.
hint: Use :split notes.txt.
why: A horizontal split opens above the current window by default.

title: Insert an equals sign between the aligned key and value columns.
hint: Start the block on the separating space, extend down two rows, then I= and Escape.
why: Block insertion places the same delimiter at one column on every selected row.

title: Indent all three statements one level.
hint: Use 3>> to shift three lines starting at the cursor.
why: A count on the doubled shift operator specifies the number of lines.

title: Delete the marked three-line draft section.

draft b

title: Delete the entire block between the header and footer, leaving those two lines.

why: Limit a broad edit with an explicit range so protected sections remain untouched.

title: Uppercase the first two columns while leaving the suffixes alone.

why: A block case operation avoids changing the rest of each identifier.

title: Open the previous buffer: the launch checklist.
after: Workspace goal: Open the previous buffer: the launch checklist.

why: Buffer order is independent of where the files appear in the project.

title: Shift the two statements right by two indentation levels.

title: Insert “// ” before all three statements.

why: Block insertion applies the typed prefix across the rectangle when you leave Insert mode.

title: Duplicate the bracketed list on the next line, including its brackets.
hint: Use ya[ to include both brackets, then j$p.
why: An around-object yank is useful when the destination needs the complete structure.

title: Fix “teh” in draft.txt, save it, and return to notes.txt.
after: Workspace goal: Fix “teh” in draft.txt, save it, and return to notes.txt.

title: Move to the lower pane, fix “teh” to “the”, and save the log.

why: Closing windows is different from deleting buffers: their files remain available.

why: Limit a broad edit with an explicit range so protected sections remain untouched.

why: Use semantic motions and a stable endpoint so each repetition starts at the next complete record.

title: Add brackets around the first word of every message.
before:
INFO ready
WARN slow
ERROR failed
hint: Insert [, move to the word end, append ], then j0.
why: Use semantic motions and a stable endpoint so each repetition starts at the next complete record.

title: Keep each first field and its last field, removing the two fields between them.
hint: Enter the second field and delete through the next two commas.
why: A counted delimiter motion removes a fixed number of fields, not characters.

title: Convert each assignment into a function call.
hint: Record f=r(, then A); and Escape. Finish with j0.
why: Character replacement preserves the value, while a separate suffix insertion closes the new syntax.

title: Mark the first word of each task as completed, keeping its description.
before:
todo write tests
waiting review docs
blocked ship release
after:
done write tests
done review docs
done ship release
hint: Record ciwdone, Escape, j0, then replay twice.
why: The replacement is constant but the original status lengths differ; an inner-word object handles the variation.

title: Change the numeric value in each setting to zero.
hint: Record f=l, ciw0, Escape, and j0.
why: The macro locates a value by its key/value separator instead of depending on the key’s width.

title: Turn each bullet into an unchecked Markdown task.
hint: Record 2li[ ] followed by a space and Escape, then j0; replay twice.
why: A consistent prefix lets a macro add a task marker without retyping the item.

title: Turn each ingredient into an unchecked shopping-list item and remove its trailing period.
hint: Remove the final period, insert the checkbox, and move down.
why: Combining a suffix cleanup with a prefix insertion avoids retyping names.

title: Replace each first word with its uppercase form and duplicate the last punctuation mark.
hint: Uppercase the word, yank the final character, and put it after itself.
why: The macro reuses each row’s own punctuation rather than assuming a fixed mark.

title: Prefix all four commands with “sudo ”.
before:
install app
restart api
reload proxy
check health
after:
sudo install app
sudo restart api
sudo reload proxy
sudo check health
hint: Record the prefix and j0 in a. @a runs it, and @@ repeats the last-used macro.
why: @@ remembers the last executed register. A count can replay that same macro several times; stop at the requested scope.

title: Turn each song and next-line duration into a set-list entry.
before:
Moon Waltz
3:20
Spoon Solo
1:05
Quiet Finale
4:00
after:
Moon Waltz (3:20)
Spoon Solo (1:05)
Quiet Finale (4:00)
hint: Append the opener, join the duration without a space, close it, and move down.
why: Each macro iteration consumes a two-line record.

title: Move each opening bracket to the start of its label and remove the colon.
hint: Prefix [, then replace the colon and original opener with a space.
why: The original closing bracket completes the new combined label.

title: Turn the quoted label into a heading and delete its next-line ID row.
before:
"Moon Room"
id=1
"Spoon Hall"
id=2
"Quiet Wing"
id=3
END
after:
# Moon Room
# Spoon Hall
# Quiet Wing
END
hint: Remove the quote boundaries, prefix the heading, then delete its ID row.
why: After deleting the ID, the next record is already under the cursor.

title: Convert each checkbox from “[ ]” to “[x]” and append “ done”.
after:
[x] build done
[x] test done
[x] ship done
hint: Record lrx and A done, end with j0, and replay twice.
why: Combining a fixed-column edit with an end-of-line append suits a consistent checklist format.

title: Convert each “name=value” row into “set name value”.
after:
set port 80
set host edge
set mode safe
hint: Record replacing = with a space, prefixing set, and moving to the next row.
why: A delimiter search handles keys of different lengths.

title: Replace the final CSV field with a quoted “ok” value.
hint: Find the last comma backward, move right, then change through line end.
why: A backward delimiter search targets the final field regardless of earlier fields.

title: Swap each “last/first” path into “first/last”.
hint: Cut the first component, discard the slash without overwriting the cut, append slash, and put.
why: Use semantic motions and a stable endpoint so each repetition starts at the next complete record.

title: Turn each two-word name into a bullet with the surname uppercase.
before:
Ada Lovelace
Grace Hopper
Alan Turing
after:
- Ada LOVELACE
- Grace HOPPER
- Alan TURING
hint: Uppercase the second word, prefix the row, then move to the next record.
why: Use a named macro register for one transformation and @@ when you want to repeat the most recently executed macro.

title: Quote each chat message but leave the speaker outside the quotes.
before:
Ada: hello
Bo: very nice
Bot: spoon located
hint: Find the message start after colon-space, insert its opener, then append its closer.
why: A delimiter-based macro preserves variable-length speaker names.

title: Duplicate each name inside angle brackets after a colon.
hint: Yank the name, append :<, put the name, append >, then j0.
why: Yank before inserting the wrapper so each record supplies its own value.

title: Turn each room into an empty haunting schedule.
hint: Wrap each whole line as a quoted key with an empty list.
why: Using line boundaries preserves room names that contain spaces.

title: Replace every quoted token with “REDACTED”.
hint: Record ci"REDACTED, Escape, and j0.
why: The quote object handles different secret lengths and leaves both delimiters intact.

title: Replace the first CSV field with “archived”.
hint: Record ct,archived, Escape, and j0.
why: The till motion keeps the comma while changing a variable-length field.

title: Replace the trailing numeric code in each row with “pending”.
hint: Record f:lCpending, Escape, and j0, then replay.
why: Changing from a semantic delimiter to line end handles different numeric widths.

title: Replace the value of each flag with “false”, keeping the inline comment.
before:
a=true # one
long=yes # two
x=1 # three
after:
a=false # one
long=false # two
x=false # three
hint: Find the value and change its word; leave the comment outside the change.
why: Use a named macro register for one transformation and @@ when you want to repeat the most recently executed macro.

title: Turn the dash-framed labels into plain badge names ending in “ badge”.
after:
VIP badge
GUEST badge
VERY IMPORTANT GOOSE badge
hint: Strip each frame and append the plain-text type.
why: The macro converts a visual frame into an explicit textual label.

title: Uppercase each label, replace its colon with “ — ”, and keep its value unchanged.
before:
info: quiet
warning: very loud
error: extremely quiet
after:
INFO — quiet
WARNING — very loud
ERROR — extremely quiet
hint: Uppercase up to the colon, then replace colon-space with the new separator.
why: The case operator stops before the value, so mixed-case data would be preserved.

title: Copy each email domain into a new parenthesized suffix.
hint: Yank from after @ through line end, then append the saved domain in parentheses.
why: Copying to line end includes the dots in each domain.

title: Move each final digit into square brackets at the start of its row.
hint: Cut the digit, put it at the beginning, frame it, then remove the old trailing space.
why: A cut can rearrange data while a macro supplies the common punctuation.

title: Turn the filenames into shell copy commands.
after:
cp report.csv backup/
cp annual-summary.csv backup/
cp notes.txt backup/
hint: Record Icp, Escape, A backup/, Escape, then j0. Replay on the other two lines.
why: I and A anchor the transformation to each row, so filename length does not matter.

title: Turn each “title | author” row into “author — title”.
before:
Moon Atlas | Ada
Tiny Maps | Bo
Big Book | Cy
after:
Ada — Moon Atlas
Bo — Tiny Maps
Cy — Big Book
hint: Cut the title, discard the delimiter, append the separator, and put the title.
why: Use the black-hole register for cleanup so it does not overwrite the cut title.

title: Convert each year/title pair into “title [year]”.
before:
1926: First Spoon
2026: Better Spoon
2126: Space Spoon
after:
First Spoon [1926]
Better Spoon [2026]
Space Spoon [2126]
hint: Cut the year, discard colon-space, append the saved year in brackets.
why: A protected cut lets one macro rearrange variable text.

title: Wrap each path in a require call.
hint: Record Irequire(" and A");, ending with j0, then repeat.
why: Boundary motions make a wrapping macro work for different path lengths.

title: Make every command backgrounded and redirect it to null.
hint: Append the suffix once while recording, then repeat on the remaining commands.
why: Record one complete record transformation, including the motion that lands on the next record.

title: Convert each path into an HTML image element.
hint: Record the opening markup, closing markup, and next-line motion.
why: Record one complete record transformation, including the motion that lands on the next record.

title: Wrap every quest title in a checkbox and add its completion marker.
before:
Find the spoon
Ask the dragon nicely
Return the spoon
after:
[x] Find the spoon — done
[x] Ask the dragon nicely — done
[x] Return the spoon — done
hint: Record both boundary insertions in b, then repeat the macro.
why: A line-oriented macro handles titles of very different lengths.

title: Convert each “name -> destination” into a destination-first command.
before:
alpha -> shelf1
beta -> shelf22
gamma -> attic
after:
shelf1 <- alpha
shelf22 <- beta
attic <- gamma
hint: Cut the name, discard arrow-space, append the reversed arrow and name, then trim the carried space.
why: Protect the cut from delimiter deletion with the black-hole register.

title: Turn each route into a GET request line with an HTTP version.
after:
GET /health HTTP/1.1
GET /users HTTP/1.1
GET /metrics HTTP/1.1
hint: Record a prefix, a suffix, and j0; replay twice.
why: Record one complete record transformation, including the motion that lands on the next record.

title: Prefix each hostname with https and append the health endpoint.
hint: Record the protocol and endpoint around each hostname.
why: Use a named macro register for one transformation and @@ when you want to repeat the most recently executed macro.

title: Turn each crew member into a radio check, preserving their name.
hint: Record the two wrappers and j0; replay twice.
why: Line boundaries work equally well for single-word and multi-word names.

title: Convert the key and next-line value into a quoted JSON property.
hint: Quote the key, add the JSON separator, join the value, and close it.
why: A good solution targets only the changed region and uses stable boundaries rather than arbitrary character counts.

title: Turn the key/value row into a Markdown table row with surrounding pipes.
hint: Replace = with the table separator, then add the outer boundaries.
why: Line-boundary insertions preserve the multi-word value.

title: Replace the entire two-line disclaimer with “No warranty.”.
before:
Header

This is provided
as is, without support.

Footer
hint: Change the inner paragraph at the cursor.
why: Use sentence, paragraph, and line boundaries to edit prose without counting every character.

title: Move the shell background marker to a comment on the same line.
hint: Replace the final ampersand with the explanatory comment.
why: Treat punctuation-rich paths as fields or WORDs; use their delimiters to preserve the surrounding command.

title: Turn the “boss defeated” message into a return value instead of a log.
hint: Remove the call opener, prefix return, and delete the closer before the semicolon.
why: Reuse the string rather than retyping it.

title: Remove the retry wrapper and append “ # once” after the deployment statement.
hint: Unwrap the call, move to the semicolon, and append the note.
why: The call and its explanation now agree that deployment happens once.

title: Turn the title and two tasks into one heading followed by numbered steps.
before:
Launch plan
pack snacks
thank goose
after:
# Launch plan
1. pack snacks
2. thank goose
hint: Prefix the title and each step in place.
why: Small boundary insertions preserve the wording while giving the note a clear structure.

title: Convert a thrown string into an Error construction.
hint: Insert the constructor before the string and close it before the semicolon.
why: A small sequence of precise edits can change syntax while preserving the original values and expressions.

title: Replace the debug call with a return of its inner expression.
hint: Remove the call prefix, insert return, and delete its closing parenthesis.
why: Starting at the first nonblank character preserves indentation.

title: Wrap only the second argument in “encode(...)”.
hint: Insert encode( before value, then close it before the next comma.
why: Delimiters identify the argument being edited more reliably than counting letters.

title: Put “wash hands” and “preheat oven” before mixing, in that order.
before:
# Moon Cake
mix batter
preheat oven
bake
after:
# Moon Cake
wash hands
preheat oven
mix batter
bake
hint: Move preheat above mixing, then open the missing first step above it.
why: Reordering an existing step and inserting a missing one completes one coherent recipe fix.

title: Turn “name: value” into a quoted JSON property with a comma.
hint: Quote the key and value, then add a trailing comma.
why: Combine small, focused operators while leaving the surrounding code untouched.

title: Replace the three-line body with an indented “return null;”.
hint: Delete the three old statements, then insert the replacement above the closer.
why: Work with complete lines when their order, indentation, or grouping is the intended change.

title: Cross out the false lead and add “ solved” to its status.
hint: Check the box, wrap the lead text, and append its status.
why: One visible completion update can involve several small boundary edits.

title: Change the robot’s empty reply into “I brought snacks.”.
hint: Change inside the first quoted value.
why: The object and the unrelated flag stay unchanged.

title: Move backup before the jump comment and label it “// safety first”.
hint: Move the backup line above the jump’s comment, then insert its own comment above it.
why: Each operation keeps its explanation attached after reordering.
